definition: Normative means relating to an ideal standard, model, or rule of behavior that things are expected to conform to.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word normative. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know normative should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The ethics committee's report made a normative argument about how researchers should treat their volunteers.
Customary is weaker than normative: a customary practice is just what people usually do, while a normative rule says what they ought to do.
Compulsory is stronger than normative: a normative standard tells you what you should do, but a compulsory rule forces you to comply.

Prescriptive means laying down rules for how things should be done — a prescriptive grammar tells you which usages to avoid. Normative is one notch more abstract: relating to standards of how things ought to be, even when no rule is issued. A claim can be normative without prescribing anything; prescriptive language always issues the rule.

Standard-setting describes whatever establishes the model others are expected to follow — a standard-setting body, a standard-setting performance. Normative describes anything concerned with such standards: claims, theories, and assumptions about how things ought to be. A standard-setting act creates the benchmark; a normative claim appeals to one.

In her philosophy seminar, Jalen's professor wrote two sentences on the board: 'Most drivers exceed the speed limit' and 'Drivers should obey the speed limit.' She explained that the first sentence merely reports a fact about the world, while the second is a normative claim, because it appeals to a standard of how people ought to behave.
For the rest of the semester, students practiced spotting the moment an argument quietly slid from facts into normative territory.
The second sentence expresses a standard of how people should act rather than reporting how they do act, which is exactly what makes it normative.
academic register (ethics, social science, linguistics)
Normative is an analytical word you will meet in essays and research, not casual talk.
Use it when a claim, theory, or standard is about how things should be, and reach for descriptive when something merely reports how things are.

The planning office released two documents about the harbor district on the same afternoon.
The first was a survey: how many people cross the bridge each day, where the noise is worst, which lots have stood empty for a decade.
The second made a normative argument — that the district ought to put housing before parking, and that a waterfront belongs to those who walk it, not to those who drive past.
At the hearing, the difference mattered.
Nobody disputed the bridge counts, but the second document drew a line of speakers, some praising its vision, others calling its ideals someone else's.
As one commissioner put it, the survey told the city what the district is; the argument told the city what it should be.
